How many topological orders does this graph have?
A → B → C → A
9.e: The edges require A before B, B before C, and C before A, which is impossible in a linear order. A visited flag alone prevents repeated DFS calls but does not prove a graph is acyclic. Rule: A topological ordering exists if and only if the directed graph is a DAG.

9.q:
After DFS from A finishes, is [A, B] a complete topological order?
Vertices: A, B, C
Edges: A → B
C is isolated.
o: Yes, because C has no edges
No; the order must also include C
No; an isolated vertex makes a cycle
Yes, if BFS also visits A
9.e: A topological ordering is a permutation of all vertices. C can appear anywhere relative to A and B, but cannot be omitted. The outer loop in topsort includes it. Rule: DFS topological sort needs an outer loop over every vertex.

9.q:
Which A-to-B path has lower total weight?
A → B: weight 0.9
A → C: weight 0.1
C → D: weight 0.1
D → B: weight 0.2
o: A → B, because it has one edge
BFS always chooses the lower-weight path
9.e: The direct path costs 0.9. The three-edge path costs 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.4. BFS minimises edge count in an unweighted graph, not a sum of differing weights. Rule: Weighted path cost is the sum of edge weights.

9.q:
For a full graph traversal, which time bounds are correct?
V vertices, E edges
Visit all components; constant-time queue/stack operations.
9.e: With adjacency lists, each vertex and each adjacency entry is processed a constant number of times. A matrix requires scanning a row of V entries for each vertex, so a full traversal costs O(V²). Rule: The familiar O(V + E) bound assumes adjacency lists.

9.q:
What is the maximum number of edges?
Simple directed graph with n vertices:
no self-loops; at most one edge for each ordered pair.
9.e: Each of n source vertices can have an edge to each of the other n − 1 vertices. Both A → B and B → A are allowed. The minimum is 0 unless connectivity is required. Rule: Simple directed graph without loops: 0 ≤ |E| ≤ n(n − 1).

9.q:
For n labelled vertices and edges i → j whenever i < j, what is true?
Vertices: 1, 2, …, n
o: The graph has a cycle and no topological order
The graph is a DAG with exactly one topological order
The graph has n! topological orders
9.e: Every edge increases the label, so there is no cycle. Every smaller label must precede every larger label, forcing the unique order 1, 2, …, n. There are n(n − 1)/2 edges. An edgeless graph instead permits n! orders. Rule: Topological orders count permutations satisfying every dependency.

10.q: Which container does uniform cost search use for its frontier?
10.e: Priority is the total path cost from the start.
w: A plain queue is the BFS frontier.
A stack is the DFS frontier.
A hash table does not order the frontier by cost.

10.q: When does uniform cost search stop?
o: When the target is first enqueued
When the queue first has two entries
10.e: Only then is its cost guaranteed to be the lowest.
w: A cheaper path might still be found.
The queue size has no relation to the target.
UCS can stop earlier, at the target.

10.q: Which strategy guarantees the lowest total weight when weights are non-negative?
10.e: It always expands the cheapest path so far.
w: It minimises edges, not weight.
It gives no guarantee about path length.
It orders a DAG and does not search for paths.

10.q: In state-space search, what does an edge represent?
o: A weight that must be summed
A legal move from one state to another
10.e: Following edges builds a sequence of actions.
w: Weights label edges but are not what an edge is.
A goal is a vertex, not an edge.
Invalid states are excluded vertices, not edges.

10.q: What is the priority of an entry in the UCS priority queue?
o: The number of edges from the start
An estimate of the remaining distance to the goal
The total path cost from the start so far
The alphabetical order of the vertex
10.e: A smaller cost means higher priority.
w: That is the BFS measure, not UCS.
That is the idea of informed search, not UCS.
Labels do not decide cost.

11.q: How many distinct round-trip tours exist for `n` cities with symmetric distances?
11.e: Divide `n!` by `n` start cities and by 2 for direction.
w: This counts every ordering, including the same tour from different starts.
This is the count when distances are asymmetric.
This is the count for an open path, not a round trip.

11.q: What is the complexity of exhaustive search for TSP?
w: This is the cost of nearest neighbour.
The number of tours grows faster than `2ⁿ`.
This is the cost of random search over `k` tours.

11.q: Which strategy always travels to the nearest unvisited city?
11.e: It makes the locally cheapest choice at every step.
w: Exhaustive search checks every tour.
Random search scores randomly chosen tours.
2-opt modifies an existing tour by exchanging edges.

11.q: What does 2-opt do to a tour?
o: Deletes 2 edges and reconnects the pieces
Builds a tour city by city
11.e: The result is a different valid tour.
w: That describes greedy construction.
That describes exhaustive search.
That describes random search.

o: A solution that no small modification improves
11.e: Local search stops there, even if a better solution exists elsewhere.
w: That is the global optimum.
The first solution need not be locally optimal.
Ties are unrelated to optimality.

o: Problems with a known polynomial-time solving algorithm
Problems that can only be verified quickly
All problems that are hard to solve
Problems solvable only in exponential time
w: That describes NP, which also contains P.
P is the efficiently solvable class, not the hard one.
Such problems are outside the known polynomial class.

12.e: It concerns polynomial-time verification of a proposed answer.
w: This is a common misreading; NP includes all of P.
The letters are not an abbreviation for this.
The letters are not an abbreviation for this.

12.q: Which relationship between P and NP is known to hold?
12.e: A solver can verify an answer by solving and comparing.
w: This would mean every verifiable problem is solvable efficiently, which is unproven.
Equality is the open question; it is unproven.
P lies inside NP, so the intersection is all of P.

12.q: What does it mean to reduce problem 1 to problem 2?
o: Convert any instance of problem 1 into an instance of problem 2
Remove constants from the Big-O of problem 1
12.e: An algorithm for problem 2 then solves problem 1.
w: The number of inputs is unrelated to a reduction.
That is simplification of Big-O, not a reduction.
Brute force is a different strategy and needs no conversion.

12.q: How is the class NP-complete defined in terms of other classes?
12.e: It is both NP-hard and in NP.
w: This would include easy problems in P.
This is just P, which is not hard.
Without membership in NP, a problem is merely NP-hard.

12.q: A classmate says: "NP means Not Polynomial, so NP problems can never be solved quickly." What is wrong with this?
o: NP stands for Nondeterministic Polynomial. It means a proposed answer can be verified in polynomial time, and every P problem is also in NP.
NP problems have been proved to need exponential time.
12.e: NP is about verifying quickly. Sorting is in NP too. For NP-complete problems we only know there is no known polynomial algorithm; nobody has proved one cannot exist.

12.q: Sorting a list of numbers in ascending order is…
o: in P, and therefore also in NP
12.e: Merge sort runs in O(n log n), so sorting is in P. Since P ⊆ NP, it is in NP as well.

12.q: Which statement is a proven fact?
o: Every problem in P is also in NP
12.e: If you can solve a problem quickly, you can verify an answer quickly by solving it yourself. Whether P = NP is still open: it is a US$1 million Millennium Prize problem.

12.q: RSA-212 (212 digits) took about 2000 CPU years to factor. Once the two factors were published, checking them…
o: needed one multiplication: a fraction of a second
needed the same trial division again
12.e: That is exactly the NP pattern: hard to solve, easy to verify. Note that factoring is in NP but is not known to be NP-complete.

12.q: Suppose someone finds a polynomial-time algorithm for TSP (the yes/no version: "is there a tour of length ≤ k?"). What follows?
o: Every NP problem could be solved in polynomial time, so P = NP.
Nothing, because TSP is unrelated to other problems.
12.e: The TSP decision problem is NP-complete. Every NP problem reduces to it, so a fast TSP algorithm plus the translation step would solve every NP problem fast.

12.q: In the HCP → TSP reduction on a graph with n = 5 vertices, the shortest tour in G′ has length 6. What does this tell you?
o: The TSP solver made a mistake.
12.e: Length 6 > n means every tour uses at least one cost-2 edge, which is not in G. So no cycle through all vertices exists using only G's edges.

12.q: Why is "find the shortest TSP tour" called NP-hard rather than NP-complete?
o: Because it is easy to solve.
It is at least as hard as NP-complete problems, but given a tour there is no known quick way to check it is the shortest, so it is not known to be in NP.
12.e: NP-complete = NP-hard and in NP. The yes/no version ("tour ≤ k?") is checkable and NP-complete; the optimisation version is NP-hard.

12.q: An O(2ⁿ) algorithm handles n = 40 in about 18 minutes. You buy a computer 1000× faster. In the same 18 minutes you can now handle about…
12.e: 2¹⁰ ≈ 1000, so 1000× more speed buys only about 10 more items. For an O(n²) algorithm the same upgrade would allow about 31× bigger inputs.

lessons.title: Counting
lessons.goal: Count how many valid outcomes a problem allows, using a small set of rules.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Counting gives the arithmetic behind "how much work?". Later chapters count loop iterations, tours and orderings.
🧠 Memory hook
One outcome first. Describe a single valid outcome, then ask: AND or OR? Order? Repetition?
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishWhat a counting question asksProduct rule (AND)Sum rule (OR)Inclusion–exclusion (overlapping OR)Complement and pigeonholePermutations (order matters)Combinations (order does not matter)Block method (objects stay together)Gap method (objects stay apart)Circular arrangementsWording guide
⚡ At a glance — the counting toolkit
Product rule (AND)Sum rule (OR)Inclusion–exclusionComplementPermutationCombinationBlockGapCircular
1.0Start here: counting is about choices, not lists

You are never asked to write out every possibility. You are asked how many there are, and the trick is to describe one outcome and count the choices at each step.

  • AND means multiply. An outfit needs a shirt and trousers and shoes. With 3, 2 and 4 options, that is 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 outfits, because each shirt can go with each pair of trousers, and so on.
  • OR means add. Lunch is either one of 5 rice dishes or one of 4 noodle dishes: 5 + 4 = 9 choices. You never eat both, so the cases do not overlap.
  • Order matters or it does not. Choosing a gold, silver and bronze medallist from 10 runners is ordered (10 × 9 × 8 = 720). Choosing a 3-person team from 10 is unordered, so the same group counted in 3! = 6 different orders collapses to 720 ÷ 6 = 120.
  • Pigeonhole is a guarantee, not a count. Drop 13 socks into 12 drawers: some drawer holds at least 2, whatever you do.
A habit that fixes most mistakes

Before touching a formula, ask three questions about one valid outcome: is it AND or OR? Does order matter? Can things repeat? The answers pick the rule for you.

1.1What a counting question asks

Every counting question asks how many different valid outcomes exist. Before using any formula, describe what one complete outcome looks like.

Three questions control almost every solution:

  • Are we completing several required stages (AND) or choosing one of several separate cases (OR)?
  • Does order matter?
  • Is repetition allowed?

Seven-step method

  • Define one outcome.
  • List the restrictions: underline "different", "at least", "exactly", "together", "not adjacent".
  • Decide AND (multiply) or OR (add).
  • Decide whether order matters.
  • Decide whether repetition is allowed.
  • Handle restrictions by direct counting, cases, complement, block or gaps.
  • Write a labelled formula, calculate, then sanity-check.
1.2Product rule (AND)

If task 1 can be done in m ways and task 2 in n ways, and both are needed, there are m × n ways to do both.

  • Binary strings of length n: each position has 2 choices and every position is needed, so 2ⁿ.
  • Arranging n distinct objects: n × (n−1) × ⋯ × 1 = n!, because each filled position leaves one fewer choice.

Three-letter codes from {A, B, C, D, E} with no repeats are 5 × 4 × 3 = 60, not 5³. The formula 5³ allows repeats such as AAA.

1.3Sum rule (OR)

If task 1 can be done in m ways or task 2 in n ways, and the cases cannot happen together, there are m + n ways to do exactly one of them.

SignalMeaningOperation
All stages needed to build one outcomeANDMultiply
One case chosen from separate possibilitiesORAdd

Do not trust the English word alone. Trace how one complete outcome is built.

1.4Inclusion–exclusion (overlapping OR)

When two cases can happen at the same time, plain addition counts the overlap twice: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|.

Integers 1–1000 divisible by 3 or 5: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467. The 66 multiples of 15 were counted in both lists.

1.5Complement and pigeonhole

Complement rule: wanted = all − unwanted. For "at least one", count the outcomes with none.

Four-character passwords from 36 symbols (A–Z, 0–9) with at least one digit: 36⁴ − 26⁴ = 1,222,640.

Pigeonhole principle: with more objects than categories, some category holds more than one. To guarantee m objects in one of k categories you need k(m−1) + 1 objects. Two students sharing a birth month needs 12 + 1 = 13.

1.6Permutations (order matters)

An ordered arrangement of r of n distinct objects: P(n, r) = n!/(n−r)!.

Filling r positions left to right leaves n, n−1, …, n−r+1 choices, all needed, so the product is n!/(n−r)!. Awarding gold, silver and bronze among 150 entrants: 150 × 149 × 148 = 3,307,800.

Swap test. If swapping two chosen items gives a different valid outcome, use a permutation.

1.7Combinations (order does not matter)

An unordered selection of r of n objects: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n−r)!) = P(n, r)/r!.

Each unordered group appears r! times in the ordered count, so dividing by r! removes the overcounting. Choosing 3 of 150 with ranking ignored: 3,307,800 / 6 = 551,300.

1.8Block method (objects stay together)
  • Merge the k required objects into one block, giving n − k + 1 outside objects.
  • Arrange the outside objects: (n − k + 1)!.
  • Arrange inside the block: k!.
  • Multiply.

Six distinct people in a row, two of them adjacent: 5! × 2! = 240.

Forgetting the internal factor k! assumes the block has only one internal order.

1.9Gap method (objects stay apart)
  • Arrange the m ordinary objects first. They create m + 1 gaps.
  • Choose gaps for the special objects: C(m+1, k).
  • Arrange the k special objects if they are distinct: k!.

Three men and three women in a line, no two women adjacent: 3! × C(4,3) × 3! = 144. If more than m + 1 special objects must be pairwise apart, the count is 0.

1.10Circular arrangements

For n distinct people at a round table, with rotations identical, the count is (n − 1)!. Fix one person, then arrange the rest relative to them.

If reflections are also identical (only neighbours matter), divide by 2: (n − 1)!/2 for n ≥ 3.

1.11Wording guide
Words in the questionFirst method to consider
and; followed by; one of eachProduct rule
either; one type or anotherSum rule
A or B, possibly bothInclusion–exclusion
at least one; not allComplement
arrange; rank; roles; positionsPermutation
choose; select; committee; groupCombination
must be adjacent; togetherBlock method
no two adjacent; separatedGap method
around a table; in a circleCircular arrangement
1.12Interactive lab

Slide the number of choices at each stage and watch the product rule build every outfit, switch between ordered and unordered selections to see why you divide by r!, and force a pigeonhole.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The ten counting methods of the course.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
Product ruleMultiplies the ways of every required stage.All stages are needed (AND).
Sum ruleAdds the ways of separate, mutually exclusive cases.Exactly one case is chosen (OR).
Inclusion–exclusionAdds two overlapping cases, then subtracts the overlap.Sum rule with a non-empty overlap.
Complement ruleSubtracts the unwanted outcomes from all outcomes.Signalled by "at least one" or "not".
Pigeonhole principleGuarantees a category with more than one object.Proves existence; it does not count outcomes.
PermutationCounts ordered selections, n!/(n−r)!.Swapping two items changes the outcome.
CombinationCounts unordered selections, n!/(r!(n−r)!).Swapping two items changes nothing.
Block methodGlues required-together objects into one unit.Multiplies by the internal arrangements.
Gap methodPlaces special objects into gaps between ordinary ones.Uses m + 1 gaps and C(m+1, k).
Circular arrangementCounts seatings with rotations identical, (n−1)!.Divides by n compared with a line.

Permutations and combinations are selection formulas built on the product rule. They are not separate rules.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1.1

Multiples of 3 or 5

The problem

How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by 3 or by 5?

The trace
  • Multiples of 3: ⌊1000/3⌋ = 333.
  • Multiples of 5: ⌊1000/5⌋ = 200.
  • Multiples of both, meaning of 15: ⌊1000/15⌋ = 66.
  • Total: 333 + 200 − 66 = 467.
The lesson

A number can satisfy both cases, so subtract the overlap once.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1.2

Together and apart in a circle

The problem

Six people sit at a round table. Two must sit together and two others must not sit next to each other.

The trace
  • Block the first pair: 5 circular objects give 4! = 24, times 2! inside the block, so 48.
  • Remove arrangements where the second pair is also together: 4 circular objects give 3! = 6, times 2! × 2!, so 24.
  • Valid arrangements: 48 − 24 = 24.
The lesson

Count the requirement first, then subtract the unwanted overlap inside it.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Licence plates. A plate begins with S, followed by two uppercase letters, four digits and one uppercase letter. How many plates are possible?
Show answer
Product rule over eight positions: 1 · 26 · 26 · 10⁴ · 26 = 26³ · 10⁴ = 175,760,000.
2
Non-taxi plates. Plates beginning with SH are reserved for taxis. How many plates remain for non-taxis?
Show answer
Subtract the reserved set: 26³·10⁴ − 26²·10⁴ = 169,000,000. With S and H fixed, one letter, four digits and a final letter vary.
3
Passwords with at least one digit. How many case-insensitive alphanumeric passwords of length 6, 7 or 8 contain at least one digit?
Show answer
Complement rule for each length k: 36ᵏ − 26ᵏ (all strings minus letters only). The lengths are mutually exclusive, so add: (36⁶−26⁶)+(36⁷−26⁷)+(36⁸−26⁸) = 2,684,483,063,360.
4
Starts with a or ends with z. Using lowercase letters and digits, how many 6-character passwords start with a or end with z?
Show answer
Inclusion–exclusion: |A| = 36⁵, |Z| = 36⁵, |A ∩ Z| = 36⁴, so 36⁵ + 36⁵ − 36⁴ = 119,252,736.
5
Keeping A, B and C together. How many permutations of A to H keep ABC consecutive? What if A, B and C stay together in any internal order?
Show answer
Treat the three letters as one block, giving six objects. Exactly ABC: 6! = 720. Any internal order: 6! · 3! = 4,320.
6
Four diners, six seats. Four diners occupy four of six distinct seats. How many seating arrangements are there?
Show answer
Order matters: P(6,4) = 6!/2! = 360. Equivalently choose then arrange: C(6,4) · 4! = 15 · 24 = 360.
7
Forming the committee. How many 7-member committees contain 3 faculty chosen from 40 and 4 students chosen from 300?
Show answer
Two independent selections, so the product rule gives C(40,3) · C(300,4) = 3,268,216,809,000.
8
No two women adjacent. How many ways can 3 men and 3 women stand in a line if no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Arrange the men (3!), which creates 4 gaps. Choose 3 of the 4 gaps and arrange the women: 3! · C(4,3) · 3! = 6 · 4 · 6 = 144, which equals 3! · P(4,3).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Multiple-choice test (Rosen 6.1 Q3). A test has 10 questions with 4 possible answers each. In how many ways can a student answer if every question is answered? If blanks are allowed?
Show answer
Every question answered: 4¹⁰. Blanks allowed: each question has 5 options, so 5¹⁰.
2
Integers 100 to 999 (Rosen 6.1 Q23). How many integers from 100 to 999 inclusive: divisible by 7; odd; with three equal digits; not divisible by 4; divisible by 3 or 4; divisible by neither 3 nor 4; divisible by 3 but not 4; divisible by 3 and 4?
Show answer
In order: 128; 450; 9; 675; 450; 450; 225; 75. For example, 3 or 4: 300 + 225 − 75 = 450, and 3 and 4 means divisible by 12, which gives 75.
3
Two licence plate formats (Rosen 6.1 Q29). How many plates can be made from either 2 letters then 4 digits, or 2 digits then 4 letters?
Show answer
Sum rule over two disjoint formats: 26²·10⁴ + 10²·26⁴ = 52,457,600.
4
Circular seating, neighbours only (Rosen 6.1 Q45). Seat six people around a circular table where two seatings are the same if everyone has the same two neighbours, ignoring left and right.
Show answer
5!/2 = 60: fix one person to remove rotations, then halve to ignore reflections.
5
Wedding photograph (Rosen 6.1 Q47). Six people stand in a row, including the bride and groom. How many ways if the bride must be next to the groom; not next to the groom; to the left of the groom?
Show answer
Next to each other: block method 5! · 2 = 240. Not next to: 720 − 240 = 480. Bride somewhere left of the groom: half of all orders, 720/2 = 360.
6
Permutations ending in a (Rosen 6.3 Q3). How many permutations of {a, b, c, d, e, f, g} end with a?
Show answer
Fix the last letter and arrange the other six: 6! = 720.
7
Alternating men and women (Rosen 6.3 Q13). A group has n men and n women. In how many ways can they stand in a row if men and women alternate?
Show answer
Choose which sex starts (2 ways), then arrange each sex: 2 · (n!)².
8
Ten coin flips (Rosen 6.3 Q19). A coin is flipped 10 times. How many outcomes are there in total, with exactly two heads, with at most three tails, and with equal heads and tails?
Show answer
Total 2¹⁰ = 1,024. Exactly two heads C(10,2) = 45. At most three tails C(10,0)+C(10,1)+C(10,2)+C(10,3) = 176. Equal heads and tails C(10,5) = 252.
9
8 men and 5 women, no two women adjacent (Rosen 6.3 Q23). How many ways can 8 men and 5 women stand in a line so that no two women are adjacent?
Show answer
Place the men first (8!), which creates 9 gaps. Place the women in gaps: P(9,5). Total 8! · P(9,5) = 609,638,400.
10
Club of 25 members (Rosen 6.3 Q27). How many ways are there to choose 4 members for an executive committee, and to choose a president, vice president, secretary and treasurer with no person holding two offices?
Show answer
Committee: order does not matter, C(25,4) = 12,650. Offices: order matters, P(25,4) = 303,600.
11
Cinema seating. 19 students occupy a row of 22 seats. How many ways? If Andrew, Brandon and Cheryl join (22 students in 22 seats) and Brandon sits at either end, how many ways?
Show answer
First part P(22,19) = 22!/3! ≈ 1.87 × 10²⁰. Second part: 2 end seats for Brandon, then the other 21 people fill 21 seats, 2 · 21! ≈ 1.02 × 10²⁰.
12
10 men and 10 women. How many ways are there to arrange them in a row? How many ways to seat all 20 at two circular tables (one blue, one red) with 5 men and 5 women alternating at each?
Show answer
Row: 20! ≈ 2.43 × 10¹⁸. Two alternating tables: (C(10,5)·C(10,5)·4!·5!/2) · (C(5,5)·C(5,5)·4!·5!/2) ≈ 1.32 × 10¹¹. The answer key says rounded values are for reference; the formula is what you must produce.
⚡ Quick examples
Permutation or combination?
PointUse the swap test on two selected items.
ExampleGold and silver swapped is a new outcome, so it is a permutation.
ExplanationA changed outcome means order matters.
Complement shortcut
Point36⁴ − 26⁴ counts passwords with at least one digit.
ExampleAll passwords minus the all-letter passwords.
ExplanationCounting "none" is far easier than counting "at least one" directly.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • Describe one outcome before choosing a formula.
  • AND multiplies; separate OR cases add; overlapping OR subtracts the overlap.
  • Order matters: P(n,r). Order ignored: C(n,r) = P(n,r)/r!.
  • Together: block, times k! inside. Apart: gaps, m + 1 of them.
  • Circle with identical rotations: (n−1)!; also identical reflections: (n−1)!/2.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
Product rule vs sum ruletap to flip
Multiply when every stage is needed; add when exactly one separate case is chosen.
Why divide by r! in C(n,r)?tap to flip
Each unordered group appears r! times in the ordered count.
Guarantee two in the same one of 12 categoriestap to flip
12 + 1 = 13 objects.
Number of gaps from m ordinary objectstap to flip
m + 1.
➡ Where next? Counting tells you how many inputs and operations exist. Next, Big-O uses counts to compare growth.

lessons.title: Complexity and Big-O
lessons.goal: Compare algorithms by how their work grows with input size, not by seconds.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Big-O lets you compare algorithms fairly, whatever the language, hardware or test input.
🧠 Memory hook
Count, then simplify. Count the iterations first. Drop constants and keep the dominant term last.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishWhat an algorithm isWhy count growth, not secondsGrowth rate and Big-OComplexity classesDominance rulesSix-step method for codeLoop patterns
⚡ At a glance — growth order, slowest-growing first
1→log n→n→n log n→n²→n³→2ⁿ→n!
2.0Start here: Big-O is about how work grows, not how long it takes

Stopwatch time depends on your laptop, your language and what else is running. Big-O ignores all that and asks one question: when the input gets bigger, how fast does the number of steps grow?

  • Doubling test. Make the input twice as big. If the steps also double, it is O(n). If they quadruple, O(n²). If they go up by just one, O(log n). If they square, you are in exponential trouble.
  • Drop the small stuff. 3n + 5 steps and n steps grow the same way as n gets huge, so both are O(n). Only the fastest-growing term matters.
  • Best, worst, average. Looking for a name in an unsorted list: with luck it is first (best case), in the worst case it is last. We usually quote the worst case because it is a promise you can rely on.
Code shapeSteps for n = 8Steps for n = 16Big-O
one loop over n816O(n)
loop inside a loop64256O(n²)
halve n until 134O(log n)
Why this matters

Every later chapter ends with “and its cost is …”. If you can count loop passes and halvings, you can read any of those costs.

2.1What an algorithm is

An algorithm is a complete specification for solving a problem. It has three parts:

  • Inputs: the data it starts with.
  • Outputs: the answer it produces.
  • A finite sequence of simple, precise, effective steps from input to output.

The form does not matter: code, pseudocode or plain steps. What matters is the input–output contract. Knuth asks for steps that are precise (unambiguous), effective (they move towards the goal) and practical (finish in reasonable time).

Property of a good algorithmMeaning
CorrectnessRight output for every valid input
Space efficiencyUses as little memory as possible
Time efficiencyRuns as fast as possible; the focus of this chapter
2.2Why count growth, not seconds

Efficiency is not about programming language, operating system, processor speed, whose implementation it is, or the size of one test input. It is about how the number of operations grows as the input grows.

InputBrute-force gcd (iterations)Repeated-subtraction gcd (iterations)
gcd(81, 36)285
gcd(330, 231)1995
gcd(1989, 867)8178

Same input and output, very different work. Brute force is not always a real option: trying every ordering of 80 localities means 80! ≈ 7.2 × 10¹¹⁸ orderings.

2.3Growth rate and Big-O

Growth rate is how the operation count grows as n grows. Big-O such as O(n²) says that for large n the work grows roughly like n². It is an upper bound on the shape of growth, not an exact count.

State what a measurement covers before giving a bound:

TermMeaning
Best caseLeast work among valid inputs of the same size
Worst caseMost work among valid inputs of the same size; the course default
Average caseExpected work under a stated distribution of inputs
Amortised timeTotal cost of a sequence of operations divided across them; no randomness assumed
Auxiliary spaceExtra memory beyond the input that exists at the same time

Worst case is the default because the best case is a special situation, and the average case needs input frequencies we usually lack. Give the tightest bound you can justify.

2.4Complexity classes
NameBig-OTypical source
ConstantO(1)Unaffected by input size
LogarithmicO(log n)Halving, as in binary search
LinearO(n)One pass over the input
LinearithmicO(n log n)Merge sort
PolynomialO(nᵏ)k = 2 quadratic, k = 3 cubic
ExponentialO(kⁿ)k constant
FactorialO(n!)Often grouped with exponential
Big-OWhen n doubles
O(1)Operations stay the same
O(log n)Operations rise by about 1
O(n)Operations double
O(n²)Operations quadruple
O(2ⁿ)Adding 1 to n already doubles the operations
O(n!)Adding 1 to n multiplies the operations by n

A machine 1000 times faster lifts the feasible size of an n! algorithm only from about 9.5 to 12.5.

2.5Dominance rules
  • Drop constant multipliers: O(7n) = O(n).
  • Keep only the dominant term of a sum: O(n² + 5n + 20) = O(n²).
  • Multiply repeated costs: n iterations of O(n) work give O(n²).

Growth order to memorise: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.

ExpressionBoundReason
1000 · 2ⁿO(2ⁿ)A fixed multiplier
0.0001 · 2.1ⁿO(2.1ⁿ)The base is not a multiplier: 2.1ⁿ / 2ⁿ = 1.05ⁿ grows without bound
5ⁿ + 2ⁿO(5ⁿ)The larger base dominates
n! · n²O(n! · n²)Factors of a product all stay
2ᵐ + 2ⁿ, or m · nO(2ᵐ + 2ⁿ), O(mn)Independent inputs cannot be compared; keep both

Constants matter for speed, not for scaling.

2.6Six-step method for code
  • Name the input size(s): n, possibly m or k.
  • Split the code into blocks: statements, loops, conditionals, calls.
  • Count each loop's iterations exactly first: n, n/2, i, log₂ n.
  • Find the cost of one iteration, including nested loops and calls. A call is not automatically O(1).
  • Combine: multiply iterations by cost per iteration, add consecutive blocks, and use a summation when cost depends on the index.
  • Simplify only at the end.
2.7Loop patterns
PatternCost
range(n), range(10, n), range(0, n, 2)O(n): constant offsets and divisors drop out
range(20)O(1)
Consecutive loops over n then mO(n + m): add
Nested independent loops over n and mO(nm): multiply
Triangular loop, inner count iΣ i = n(n+1)/2, so O(n²)
i = i * 2 or i = i // 2About log₂ n iterations: O(log n)
Inner work about n/i for each in · Hₙ, so O(n log n)

The log base never matters: changing base only adds a constant factor, so O(log₂ n) = O(log₃ n). Careful: log(n²) = 2 log n is O(log n), but (log n)² is not.

An early-return search has a best case of O(1) and a worst case of O(n). Always state which one you mean.

2.8Interactive lab

Pick a loop shape, drag n, and watch the step count. Each row doubles n and shows the multiplier, which is how Big-O is read off in practice.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The seven complexity classes, in increasing order of growth.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ConstantO(1): work independent of n.No loop over the input.
LogarithmicO(log n): the problem shrinks by a constant factor each step.Halving loops.
LinearO(n): work proportional to n.One pass.
LinearithmicO(n log n): n work at each of log n levels.Between linear and quadratic.
PolynomialO(nᵏ) for constant k.The variable is in the base.
ExponentialO(kⁿ) for constant k.The variable is in the exponent.
FactorialO(n!).Grows faster than every kⁿ.

Quadratic and cubic are polynomial with k = 2 and k = 3. They are not separate classes.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2.1

Triangular loop

The problem

An outer loop runs i from 1 to n; the inner loop runs i times with constant work.

The trace
  • Inner iterations per i: i.
  • Total: 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n+1)/2.
  • Dominant term: n²/2; drop the constant. Result: O(n²).
The lesson

When the inner cost depends on the index, write a summation instead of multiplying.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2.2

Constant offset and divisor

The problem

Compare range(n), range(10, n) and range(0, n, 2).

The trace
  • Iterations: n, n − 10 and n/2.
  • Every one is a constant multiple or offset of n.
The lesson

Count exactly first. Constants then drop out and all three are O(n).

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Complexity of an exam-style recursion. What is the time complexity of z(n) when each call loops n times calling z(n-1)?
Show answer
T(n) = n · T(n−1), which unrolls to n!, so O(n!).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Counting steps from a table. A table gives, for each input value, the number of times an operation is performed (the count is the input plus a constant). What is the Big O?
Show answer
O(n): the number of operations grows linearly with the input, and the constant offset is dropped.
2
Simplify the step counts. Give the Big O of: (a) 9 + 0.02N² + 0.1N, (b) N² + 2N − 3, (c) N! + 100N²⁰, (d) 2ᴺ + N!, (e) 5N log₂N + N√N, (f) N² log₂N + N (log₂N)², (h) 10⁵ + 10⁴(log N)² + 10³ log N².
Show answer
(a) O(N²); (b) O(N²); (c) O(N!); (d) O(N!); (e) O(N^1.5) because N√N beats N log N; (f) O(N² log N); (h) O((log N)²). Keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constants.
3
Three loop shapes. Give the complexity of: two loops in a row over n and m; a nested n × n loop followed by a single n loop; and a loop where the inner while j > i runs from n down to i.
Show answer
Two loops in a row: O(n + m) or O(max(n, m)). Nested then single: O(n²). Dependent inner loop: n + (n−1) + … + 1, so O(n²).
4
f, g and h. f(n) sums 1..n−1 in a loop. g(n) loops i from 1 to n−1 and calls f(i) each time. h(n) returns f(n) + g(n). Give each complexity.
Show answer
f is O(n). g calls an O(i) function n times: 1 + 2 + … + n, so O(n²). h is O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²).
5
Cost of a nested call. func_a has two nested loops of size n and calls f(j) inside. What is its complexity if f costs a constant T, and if f(j) costs j time units?
Show answer
Constant T: n² · T = O(n²). Linear f(j) = j: n · (0 + 1 + … + (n−1)) = n · n(n−1)/2, which is O(n³).
6
Helper call inside loops. sub_func(n) is called inside: func_6a (for i in range(n), for j in range(i)); func_6b (for i in 1..n, for j in 1..i²); func_2c (for i, for j, if j % i == 0, for k in 1..n).
Show answer
The answer key gives O(n³), O(n⁴) and O(n³ log n), which is what you get when sub_func(n) costs O(n): 6a runs it n(n−1)/2 times; 6b runs it Σi² ≈ n³/3 times; in 2c the if is true about n/i times per i, a harmonic sum n log n, and each hit runs n calls of cost n.

PointKeep only the fastest-growing term.
Examplen log n + n simplifies to O(n log n).
ExplanationFor large n, the lower terms become negligible.
Halving loop

  • Order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.

lessons.title: Searching and Sorting
lessons.goal: Reason about loops, then compare linear and binary search, and insertion and merge sort.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
A smarter algorithm changes the growth rate, which no faster hardware can do.
🧠 Memory hook
Halve it. Binary search and merge sort win by halving: log n steps instead of n.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishReasoning about any iterative algorithmLinear searchBinary searchLinear against binary searchInsertion sortMerge sort (bottom-up)Insertion sort against merge sort
⚡ At a glance — four algorithms
Linear search O(n)Binary search O(log n)Insertion sort O(n²)Merge sort O(n log n)
3.0Start here: three everyday ideas behind searching and sorting
  • Linear search = reading a shelf left to right. You look at every book until you find it. Simple, works on any shelf, but a long shelf takes a long time.
  • Binary search = the “higher or lower” guessing game. If the shelf is sorted, open it in the middle, decide which half the book must be in, and throw the other half away. Each guess halves what is left, so 1,000 books need about 10 guesses.
  • Insertion sort = sorting playing cards in your hand. Pick up the next card and slide it left past bigger cards until it fits.
  • Merge sort = merging two sorted piles. Two already-sorted piles merge easily: repeatedly take the smaller top card. So split the pile, sort the halves, merge.
What is a loop invariant?

A promise about your variables that is true every time the loop comes round. In insertion sort: “the cards in my left hand are sorted”. If the promise holds at the start, holds after every pass, and the loop ends, then the final state is correct.

3.1Reasoning about any iterative algorithm

A useful loop makes progress towards finishing. Ask four questions of any iterative algorithm:

  • State: which variables describe the current situation? Examples: low and high; the sorted-prefix boundary i.
  • Progress: what changes in one iteration? The region shrinks, or the sorted prefix grows by one.
  • Invariant: which fact stays true before and after every iteration? Examples: "if the key exists it lies between low and high"; "a[0:i] is sorted".
  • Stopping rule: exactly when does the loop finish?

Tracing by hand

  • Copy the input and label every index.
  • Write the initial values of the important variables.
  • Execute one iteration only.
  • Record every changed variable.
  • Check the stopping condition before the next row.
3.2Linear search

Start at the beginning and compare items one by one until the key is found or the collection ends. It returns the index, or -1 on failure.

  • Unsuccessful search: every item is checked, so n comparisons.
  • Successful search: 1 comparison at best, n at worst, and (n + 1)/2 on average.
  • Complexity: O(n). No precondition on the order.
3.3Binary search

Linear search removes one candidate per comparison. Binary search removes half, but needs a sorted array. Look at the middle item and discard the half that cannot contain the key.

python
def binary_search(a, k): # a must be sorted lower, upper = -1, len(a) # region is a[lower+1 .. upper-1] while upper > lower + 1: # region not empty mid = (lower + upper) // 2 if a[mid] == k: return mid elif k < a[mid]: upper = mid else: lower = mid return -1

Convention: lower is one index below the region and upper one above it. The region is empty exactly when upper == lower + 1, which is the failure condition.

Reducing n to 1 by halving takes m steps where 2ᵐ ≈ n, so m = log₂ n. Worst case log₂ n + 1 steps, so O(log n). Best case O(1).

3.4Linear against binary search
Linear searchBinary search
PreconditionNoneArray must be sorted
StrategyScan left to rightHalve the region each step
Best caseO(1)O(1)
Worst case, sorted arrayO(n)O(log n)
Unsorted arrayO(n)Not applicable
Comparisons for n = 15Up to 15Up to about 4

Both have an O(1) best case, so the worst case separates them.

3.5Insertion sort

The invariant is that the left part of the array is already sorted. The item being placed is the key. Slide it left past every larger item and drop it into place, like sorting a hand of cards.

python
def insertion_sort(a): for i in range(1, len(a)): # a[0:i] is already sorted key = a[i] j = i - 1 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j + 1] = a[j] # slide larger items right j -= 1 a[j + 1] = key
  • The outer loop calls an inner loop, so insertion sort has nested loops.
  • Worst case: a strictly reverse-ordered array. Every key slides to the front, giving n(n−1)/2 potential comparisons, so O(n²).
  • Best case: an already sorted array. Each key needs one comparison, so O(n).
3.6Merge sort (bottom-up)

Merge sort applies the divide-and-conquer idea to sorting. This chapter uses the iterative, bottom-up version: start from groups of size 1 and merge neighbouring sorted groups. The group size gs doubles at each level: 1, 2, 4, 8, …

python
def merge(left, right): out, i, j = [], 0, 0 while i < len(left) and j < len(right): if left[i] <= right[j]: # tie: take from left first out.append(left[i]); i += 1 else: out.append(right[j]); j += 1 return out + left[i:] + right[j:]
  • Going from size 1 to size n takes log₂ n levels.
  • At every level, the merges together touch every element once: n elements per level.
  • Total work: n × log₂ n, so O(n log n) in the best and worst case alike.

Merging sorted lists of lengths n and m takes O(n + m): every step advances one index and never moves backwards.

3.7Insertion sort against merge sort
Insertion sortMerge sort
StrategyNested loops, slide items leftDivide and conquer, bottom-up merge
Worst caseO(n²)O(n log n)
Best caseO(n), already sortedO(n log n): always does full merges
On an already sorted arrayFewer comparisonsStill does its full n log n work

Sorting first and then doing an O(n) scan costs O(n log n) in total, because the sorting term dominates.

3.8Interactive lab

Step linear search, insertion sort and bottom-up merge sort one decision at a time. The array, the comparison count and the pseudocode line that is running all update together.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four questions for any iterative algorithm.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
StateThe variables that describe where the algorithm is now.A snapshot, not a rule.
ProgressWhat changes in one iteration.A change, not a fact.
InvariantA fact true before and after every iteration.Justifies correctness.
Stopping ruleThe exact condition that ends the loop.Decides termination.

The invariant is not the stopping rule: one says what stays true, the other says when to stop.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3.1

Binary search for 57

The problem

Search [4, 10, 22, 35, 36, 57, 65, 71, 79, 83, 87, 89, 90, 91, 93] (n = 15) for 57.

The trace
Steploweruppermida[mid]Action
1−11577157 < 71, so upper = 7
2−1733557 > 35, so lower = 3
337557Found
The lesson

Three comparisons suffice for 15 items, because each one halves the region.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3.2

Merging with a tie rule

The problem

Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], keeping both 9s and taking from A first on a tie.

The trace
Front valuesTakeOutput so far
2, 4A: 2[2]
9, 4B: 4[2, 4]
9, 9A: 9 (tie)[2, 4, 9]
15, 9B: 9[2, 4, 9, 9]
15, 12B: 12[2, 4, 9, 9, 12]
15, 28A: 15[2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15]
23, 28A: 23[… , 23]
31, 28B: 28[… , 28]
A endsCopy A: 31[2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]
The lesson

Taking the smaller front value is safe: both inputs are sorted, so nothing smaller can hide behind either front.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
First index with a[index] ≥ key. Correct first_at_least(a, key) so it returns the first index where a[index] ≥ key, or None. Trace keys 8, 20 and 40 on a = [3, 8, 8, 14, 19, 27, 31] and state time and space.
Show answer
Keep ans. If a[mid] >= key, save ans = mid and search left (high = mid − 1); otherwise low = mid + 1. Return ans after the loop. Results: key 8 gives index 1; key 20 gives index 5 (a[5] = 27, a[4] = 19); key 40 gives None because ans is never updated. Time O(log n), space O(1). The original bug moved right after a valid value and returned an index even when nothing qualified.
2
Run-length encoding in one pass. Convert [4, 4, 4, 7, 7, 2, 2, 2, 2, 9] into [(4, 3), (7, 2), (2, 4), (9, 1)], handling empty input and explaining the final append.
Show answer
State: value, count, out. Start value, count = a[0], 1. Equal next item: count += 1. Different: append (value, count) and restart. A run is appended only when a change is seen, so the last run must be appended once after the loop. Time O(n), working space O(1), output space O(r) for r runs.
3
Merge two sorted arrays, keeping duplicates. Merge A = [2, 9, 15, 23, 31] and B = [4, 9, 12, 28], taking from A first on a tie.
Show answer
Compare A[i] with B[j]; take A[i] when A[i] <= B[j], else B[j]; advance only the index used; copy leftovers. Result [2, 4, 9, 9, 12, 15, 23, 28, 31]. At most n + m values are appended: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) output space.
4
Count inversions with nested loops. For a = [7, 2, 6, 3, 5], compare every pair i < j and count the pairs with a[i] > a[j].
Show answer
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 so each pair is compared once. Inversions: (7,2), (7,6), (7,3), (7,5), (6,3), (6,5), so the count is 6. Comparisons n(n−1)/2, time O(n²), working space O(1).
5
Search a row-and-column sorted matrix. Start at the top-right cell and find 13. Move left when the current value is larger than the target and down when it is smaller.
Show answer
If the current value is too large, its whole column below is larger, so move left. If it is too small, its whole row to the left is smaller, so move down. For target 13 the path is 18, 10, 15, 9, 13, found at row 2, column 1 (zero-based). Each comparison discards a row or column: at most r + c − 1 checks, O(r + c) time, O(1) space.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Linear against binary search counts. x = [8, 9, 11, 16, 32, 37, 43, 45, 52, 55, 58, 61, 63, 66, 68, 82, 95, 99]. How many elements do linear and binary search check to find 8, 16 and 50?
Show answer
Key 8: 1 and 4. Key 16: 4 and 2. Key 50 (absent): 18 and 5.
2
Modify linear search for duplicates. Return (a) the number of occurrences of k, (b) the index of the second occurrence or None, (c) the index of the last occurrence or None.
Show answer
(a) Do not return inside the loop; keep count += 1 and return count after it. (b) Increment count on a match and return i when count == 2; otherwise None. (c) Remember the latest matching index in last_index and return it after the loop, or scan from the back and return the first match.
3
Insertion sort, descending. Change the insertion sort to sort in descending order. What are its best and worst cases?
Show answer
Change the shifting condition to while position > 0 and value > list[position-1]. Best case O(n) when the input is already in descending order. Worst case O(n²) when it is in ascending order.
4
Merge sort just before the final merge. What does x look like just before the final merge for [96, 80, 88, 34, 47, 65, 52, 73], [62, 77, 18, 48, 64, 45, 34, 88, 82, 87, 17] and [27, 92, 93, 91, 35, 22, 31]?
Show answer
The two halves are sorted and not yet merged: [34, 80, 88, 96, 47, 52, 65, 73]; [18, 34, 45, 48, 62, 64, 77, 88, 17, 82, 87]; [27, 91, 92, 93, 22, 31, 35].
5
Maximum of a shifted sorted array. A sorted array A is shifted right by k to give Aₖ. Find the maximum when k is known in O(1), when k is unknown in O(N), and when k is unknown in O(log N).
Show answer
Known k: the original maximum at index n−1 moves to ((n−1) + k) % n = (k−1) % n, so read that index in O(1). Unknown k, O(N): linear scan until an element is larger than its right neighbour. Unknown k, O(log N): binary search; if the middle element is bigger than the one to its right, it is the maximum, otherwise move toward the side that contains the break.
6
Find the missing integer. B holds n distinct integers from 1 to n + 1 with exactly one missing. Find it with the lowest complexity.
Show answer
Four approaches in the answer key: search for each number in turn, O(n²); sort then find the gap, O(n log n); compare the sum with 1 + 2 + … + (n+1), O(n) time and O(1) space; or a flag array, O(n).

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.goal: Decompose a problem with self-calls, trace calls, and derive Big-O from a recurrence.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Recursion is a second way to decompose problems, and recurrences let you cost it exactly.
🧠 Memory hook
Calls go down, values come up. Trace in two phases, and read the recurrence from one call.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishWhat recursion isThree safety questionsTracing in two phasesBranching recursion: FibonacciHalving is not automatically O(log n)RecurrencesCommon mistakes
⚡ At a glance — the four parts of a recursive function
Contract→Base case→Reduction step→Combination step
4.0Start here: recursion in plain words

A function is recursive if it solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Think of nested Russian dolls: you open a doll, find a smaller doll, and keep going until you reach the tiny solid one.

  • Base case = the tiny solid doll. The smallest input, answered directly without any more calls. No base case means the dolls never stop.
  • Reduction = open the next doll. Every call must hand a strictly smaller problem to the next one.
  • Combination = put the dolls back. Each call waits for its smaller answer, then finishes its own bit (multiply by n, add n, take the max…) and returns.
  • The call stack is a pile of sticky notes. Each unfinished call is a note saying “I am waiting for the answer to…”. Calls go down the pile until the base case, then answers come back up one note at a time.
PhaseWhat happens for fact(3)
Going downfact(3) waits for fact(2), which waits for fact(1), which waits for fact(0)
Base casefact(0) returns 1 straight away
Coming upfact(1) = 1 × 1, fact(2) = 2 × 1, fact(3) = 3 × 2 = 6
The trust trick

When writing a recursive function, do not trace every call in your head. Assume the call on the smaller input already works and ask only: given that answer, what does this call add?

4.1What recursion is

Recursion applies decomposition by letting a function call itself on a smaller instance of the same problem. A correct recursive function has four parts:

  • Contract: one sentence stating exactly what f(input) returns.
  • Base case: the smallest input(s) answered directly, with no further call.
  • Reduction step: how the problem shrinks, such as n → n−1 or n → n//2.
  • Combination step: how the smaller answer builds the current answer.
python
def factorial(n): if n == 1: # base case return 1 return n * factorial(n - 1) # reduction and combination in one line

Here the reduction and combination share one line: n! = n × (n−1)!, with base case 1! = 1.

4.2Three safety questions
  • Is every smallest valid input handled? There may be more than one base case.
  • Does every call make progress towards a base case?
  • Can a call jump past the base case? If the base case is n == 1 but n = 0 is possible, subtracting 1 never lands on 1.

Infinite recursion means the base case is missing, unreachable, or placed after an unconditional recursive call. Python raises RecursionError after about 1000 nested calls.

4.3Tracing in two phases

A recursive call pauses the caller. Each unfinished call keeps its own parameters in a stack frame.

  • Phase A, calls go down: write each call, indent, and stop at a base case.
  • Phase B, values come up: start from the base value, substitute it into the paused caller, and continue upwards.
Calls going downValues returning up
factorial(4) waits for factorial(3)factorial(1) returns 1
factorial(3) waits for factorial(2)factorial(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2
factorial(2) waits for factorial(1)factorial(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6
factorial(1) is the base casefactorial(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24

Four calls, but only three multiplications: the base case does none. Recursion depth is the longest chain of simultaneously unfinished calls, and it sets the memory used.

4.4Branching recursion: Fibonacci

Fibonacci needs two base cases. Because each call makes two recursive calls, trace it as a call tree: in fibonacci(4), fibonacci(2) is computed twice.

python
def fibonacci(n): if n == 0: return 0 # two base cases: if n == 1: return 1 # fib(n-2) can land on either return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2) def fib_iter(n): # keeps only the last two values: O(n) a, b = 0, 1 for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a + b return a
  • The number of additions grows like 1.6ⁿ, with ratios settling near the golden ratio 1.618. Since 1.6ⁿ < 2ⁿ, both O(1.6ⁿ) and O(2ⁿ) are valid upper bounds.
  • The loop version runs n − 1 times: O(n).

Recursion is not automatically more efficient than iteration. It is a different way of expressing a solution.

4.5Halving is not automatically O(log n)
VersionCalls per levelResult
Reduce the exponent by 1One call, a chain16 multiplications for n = 16: O(n)
Halve the exponent, call twiceTwo callsT(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) = O(n); 47 multiplications for n = 16
Halve the exponent, save and reuse the half-powerOne callT(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n); 6 multiplications for n = 16

Halving gives O(log n) only when there is one recursive call per level. Writing the same call twice runs it twice, independently, unless you save the result.

4.6Recurrences

Let T(n) be the running time for input size n. Read one non-base invocation and work through these steps:

  • Name the input size and the base-case cost.
  • Count the recursive calls of one invocation, and write each smaller input size.
  • Compute the local work: what the current call does outside its recursive calls. Never count a recursive call as O(1); write it as T(smaller).
  • Write the recurrence, expand or draw the levels, sum the work, and only then simplify.
RecurrenceExpansionResult
T(n) = T(n−1) + cc + c + ⋯, n timesO(n)
T(n) = T(n/2) + clog₂ n calls of O(1)O(log n)
T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n)n + (n−1) + ⋯ + 1 = n(n+1)/2O(n²)
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n)n + n/2 + n/4 + ⋯ < 2nO(n), not O(n log n)
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)Calls double while sizes halveO(n)

Always substitute the actual argument passed to an expensive helper at each level. A helper called on a fixed size k while n halves costs O(k log n).

4.7Common mistakes
SymptomCauseRepair
Crashes immediately, counting past 0No base caseTest the smallest input before recursing
Crashes though a base case is visibleBase case written after an unconditional recursive callMove the base-case test first
Every traceback line shows the same argumentReduction step forgottenWrite out the sequence of arguments by hand
Works for even n, not oddStep size jumps over the base caseUse an inequality or cover both parities
Answer is NoneA recursive value computed but never returnedEnd every branch with return
Answer always equals the base valueRecursive line omits its own part, such as n *Re-read the combination step
Small inputs misbehaveA second base case is missingList every smallest input the reduction can reach
4.8Interactive lab

Pick factorial, sum or Fibonacci, choose n and step through the calls. Watch frames pile onto the call stack on the way down and resolve on the way up, and see memoisation remove the repeated Fibonacci calls.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The four parts of every recursive function.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
ContractStates in one sentence what f(input) returns.A sentence, not code.
Base caseAnswers the smallest input directly, with no call.Makes the recursion stop.
Reduction stepShrinks the problem to a smaller instance of the same problem.Makes progress towards the base case.
Combination stepUses the smaller answer to build the current answer.Runs after the call returns.

The stack frame is not one of the four parts. It is where an unfinished call keeps its parameters while it waits.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4.1

Counting calls and operations

The problem

Trace factorial(4) and count calls and multiplications.

The trace
  • Calls going down: factorial(4), (3), (2), (1): four calls.
  • Values coming up: 1, then 2 × 1 = 2, 3 × 2 = 6, 4 × 6 = 24: three multiplications.
The lesson

The number of calls is not the number of operations; the base case does no multiplication.

WORKED EXAMPLE 4.2

Fibonacci additions

The problem

Count the additions made by recursive Fibonacci.

The trace
nAdditions
32
44
57
833
1088
The lesson

The count grows by a factor near 1.6 per step, which is exponential.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Cost of power1. power1(x, n) returns 1 when n == 0, otherwise x * power1(x, n-1). How many multiplications for x = 3, n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
16 multiplications, one per call down to n = 0. Complexity O(n).
2
Cost of power2. power2(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; for even n it returns power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2); for odd n it returns x * power2(x, n//2) * power2(x, n//2). How many multiplications for n = 16, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
Two recursive calls per level, so the instances double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 at n = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0. Multiplications: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16×2 + 32×0 = 47. An odd n costs 2 multiplications, an even n costs 1, and n = 0 costs 0. In general at most 2(n−1) + 2n multiplications, so O(n). Calling the halved problem once and reusing the result (power3) removes the doubling.
3
Merge sort just before the final merge. For [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5] and [52, 30, 98, 59, 67, 4, 64, 12, 79], give the array just before the final merge for the bottom-up and top-down versions.
Show answer
First array. Top-down (mid = len//2): the halves [26, 34, 64] and [83, 2, 5] are sorted first, giving [26, 34, 64, 2, 5, 83]. Bottom-up: runs of 4 and 2 remain, giving [26, 34, 64, 83, 2, 5]. Second array. Top-down: [30, 52, 59, 98, 4, 12, 64, 67, 79]. Bottom-up: [4, 12, 30, 52, 59, 64, 67, 98, 79], the last merge joining a run of 8 with a single element. The two versions reach different intermediate states, so say which version you are tracing.
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Pascal triangle recursion. Complete pt(n, k), where pt(n, k) = pt(n−1, k−1) + pt(n−1, k) and the first and last entries of each level are 1. Then trace pt(4, 2).
Show answer
if k == 1: return 1; if k == n + 1: return 1; return pt(n-1, k-1) + pt(n-1, k). pt(4, 2) = pt(3, 1) + pt(3, 2) = 1 + (pt(2, 1) + pt(2, 2)) = 1 + (1 + 2) = 4.
2
power3 with one recursive call. power3(x, n) returns 1 for n == 0; otherwise it computes temp = power3(x, n//2) and returns temp * temp for even n, or x * temp * temp for odd n. How many multiplications for x = 3 with n = 16 and n = 19, and what is the complexity?
Show answer
n = 16: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6. n = 19: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8. There are up to log₂ n + 1 instances with at most 2 multiplications each, so O(log n).
3
Recursive calls with a linear helper. sub_function is linear. What is the complexity of my_function(n) when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n//2); when it calls sub_function(k) with my_function(k, n//2); and when it calls sub_function(n) then my_function(n-1)?
Show answer
O(n): n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n. O(k log n): log n levels, each costing O(k). O(n²): n + (n−1) + … + 1.
4
Recursive maximum. Write a recursive max_array(a) without sorting.
Show answer
Slicing version: if len(a) == 1: return a[0], otherwise return max(a[0], max_array(a[1:])). A faster-copying version passes lower and upper: base cases when the range is empty or has one value, otherwise mid = (lower + upper) // 2 and return max(max_array(a, lower, mid), max_array(a, mid, upper)). Both are O(n) in the worst case, since every element must be examined.
5
Recursive palindrome. Write a recursive is_palindrome(s).
Show answer
Compare the first and last characters. Base cases: length 0 or 1 gives True; a mismatch gives False. Otherwise recurse on s[1:len(s)-1]. An index version keeps i and stops when i > len(s) − 1 − i. Worst case O(n).
6
Sign-alternating recurrence. f(n) returns 1 for n 0 or 1, otherwise −f(n−1) − f(n−2). Give f(1), f(5), f(6), f(330) and the worst-case complexity.
Show answer
f(1) = 1, f(5) = −2, f(6) = 1, f(330) = 1 (the values repeat with period 3: 1, 1, −2). Each call makes two calls on n−1 and n−2, so the worst case is exponential, about O(1.6ⁿ) or O(2ⁿ).

lessons.goal: Use stacks, queues and priority queues, and cost them with an array.
lessons.html:
💡 Why it matters
Data structures decide which operations are cheap. A stack is what powers recursion.
🧠 Memory hook
Stack = LIFO, queue = FIFO. Only one end is accessible, and the cost depends on which end of the array it is.
🗺️ Roadmap of this chapter
Start here: plain EnglishAbstract data typesLinear structuresStack: push, pop, peekQueue: enqueue, dequeue, peekPriority queueLink back to recursion
⚡ At a glance — three linear structures
Stack: last in, first outQueue: first in, first outPriority queue: best priority out
5.0Start here: stacks, queues and why they matter

A data structure is just a way of arranging information so that certain jobs are quick. Different jobs need different arrangements, the same way you keep plates in a pile but people in a line. This chapter has three of them, and each is named after something you already know:

  • Stack = a pile of plates. You can only touch the top plate. push puts a plate on top, pop takes the top plate off and hands it to you, peek just looks at it. The last plate you put on is the first one you take off, so we say LIFO (last in, first out). Real examples: the Undo button and the browser Back button.
  • Queue = the line at a canteen. A new person joins at the back (enqueue); the person at the front is served first (dequeue). First come, first served: FIFO (first in, first out).
  • Priority queue = hospital triage. The most urgent patient goes first, even if they arrived last. "Best priority" might mean the smallest number or the largest, so the question always tells you which.
ActionStack (top is on the right)What you get back
push 1[1]–
push 2[1, 2]–
push 3[1, 2, 3]–
pop[1, 2]3 (the last one in)
pop[1]2
ActionQueue (front is on the left)What you get back
enqueue A[A]–
enqueue B[A, B]–
enqueue C[A, B, C]–
dequeue[B, C]A (the first one in)
In plain words: what is an "abstract data type"?

It is a menu, not a recipe. A vending machine gives you buttons and you do not care what is inside. A stack promises push, pop and peek; whether it is built from a list or something else is hidden. That is why the inside can be changed without breaking the code that uses it.

5.1Abstract data types

An abstract data type (ADT) is defined by the operations it supports, not by how they are implemented. The representation is hidden from the client.

  • Localisation: changing the implementation does not break code that uses the ADT.
  • Flexibility: different implementations can be swapped in without the client noticing.

The List ADT supports create, insert, retrieve, remove and count at a position.

5.2Linear structures

In a linear data structure only one end is accessible.

StructureAccessible itemOrder
StackThe most recently added itemLIFO: last in, first out
QueueThe earliest added item still presentFIFO: first in, first out
5.3Stack: push, pop, peek

A stack exposes only its top. Push places an item on top, pop removes and returns the top, and peek inspects the top without removing it. Examples: backspace, browser back and the function call stack.

  • With a list whose top is index 0, push and pop cost O(n) because every item shifts.
  • With the top at the end of the list, append() and pop() cost O(1). The course Stack class uses the end.

Balanced braces: push each opening bracket. On a closing bracket, pop and check that the type matches. Fail if a closing bracket arrives too early, the type does not match, or openings remain at the end.

Why is one end cheap and the other costly?

A list is a row of numbered boxes. Take the item from the back: nothing else moves, so it is one step, O(1). Take the item from the front: every other item has to shuffle one box to the left to close the gap, so it is n steps, O(n). That is why the stack keeps its top at the end of the list.

Balanced brackets, step by step

Each closing bracket must match the most recent opener that has not been closed yet. "Most recent" is exactly what a stack gives you.

ReadActionStack after
(push[ ( ]
[push[ ( , [ ]
]pop gives [ , which matches[ ( ]
)pop gives ( , which matches[ ]

The stack is empty at the end, so the text is balanced. For ( ], the ] pops a (, which does not match, so it fails.

The same idea as pseudocode, written in Python so you can read and run it. The stack keeps its top at the end of the list:

python
class Stack: def __init__(self): self.items = [] # the top of the stack is the END of the list def push(self, x): self.items.append(x) # O(1) def pop(self): return self.items.pop() # O(1): removes and returns the LAST item def peek(self): return self.items[-1] # look at the top, do not remove it def is_empty(self): return len(self.items) == 0

Balanced brackets with a stack:

python
def balanced(text): pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"} stack = [] for ch in text: if ch in "([{": stack.append(ch) # an opener: remember it elif ch in ")]}": if not stack: # a closer arrived too early return False if stack.pop() != pairs[ch]: # the MOST RECENT opener must match return False return len(stack) == 0 # openers left over = not balanced # balanced("( [ ] )") -> True balanced("( ]") -> False
5.4Queue: enqueue, dequeue, peek

A queue removes at its head (oldest item) and inserts at its tail. Enqueue adds to the tail, dequeue removes and returns the head, and peek inspects the head. Examples: a checkout line and printer job spooling.

  • With a plain array whose head is index 0, enqueue is O(1) but dequeue is O(n), because the remaining items shift down.
  • Whichever end is removable, array operations at that end cost O(n).

Palindrome check: push and enqueue the same characters. The stack reverses order and the queue preserves it, so comparing pop against dequeue tests the palindrome. O(n) time and O(n) extra space.

A queue built on a plain list. The head is index 0, so removing it makes everything else shift:

python
class Queue: def __init__(self): self.items = [] # head = index 0, tail = the END of the list def enqueue(self, x): self.items.append(x) # O(1): add at the tail def dequeue(self): return self.items.pop(0) # O(n): every other item shifts one place left def peek(self): return self.items[0] # the head, without removing it
5.5Priority queue

A priority queue is not first in, first out: dequeue and peek return the item with the best priority, whatever its arrival order. State the priority direction and a tie rule first.

Implementationenqueuepeekdequeue
Unsorted listO(1)O(n): scan for the bestO(n): scan, then delete
Sorted list, best at one endO(n): find and shiftO(1)O(1)
Binary search treeO(log n) average, O(n) worstO(1)O(log n) average, O(n) worst
Min-heapO(log n)O(1)O(log n)

No choice is best for every access pattern. If you enqueue rarely and dequeue often, a sorted list pays the ordering cost once per insertion and gets O(1) removals.

5.6Link back to recursion

A stack is what implements the call stack. A recursive function can be rewritten with an explicit stack that holds its pending parameters. Binary search pushes one branch per iteration, so its stack stays small, matching its O(log n) depth.

A queue from two stacks. Use IN for arriving items and OUT for leaving items. When OUT is empty, pop everything from IN and push it onto OUT, which reverses the order a second time. Popping OUT then returns the oldest item. One dequeue may cost O(n), but each item moves from IN to OUT only once, so the cost is amortised O(1).

Two stacks making a queue, step by step

Enqueue A, B, C: they go onto IN, so IN holds A, B, C with C on top. Now dequeue: OUT is empty, so pop everything off IN and push it onto OUT: C goes first, then B, then A. Now A is on top of OUT. Pop it: A, the oldest item, as a queue should return. The newest-on-top order was flipped by the second stack. Items only move when OUT is empty, so each item moves at most once. That is the "amortised O(1)" claim.

A queue made from two stacks:

python
class TwoStackQueue: def __init__(self): self.inbox = [] # IN: new arrivals self.outbox = [] # OUT: items ready to leave def enqueue(self, x): self.inbox.append(x) # always O(1) def dequeue(self): if not self.outbox: # refill ONLY when OUT is empty while self.inbox: self.outbox.append(self.inbox.pop()) # this flips the order return self.outbox.pop() # the oldest item is now on top
5.7Interactive lab

Operate a stack and a queue yourself, see which item is reachable, count how many items a list-based dequeue has to shift, and trace the balanced-brackets algorithm character by character.

🔤 Exact names — know these word for word
The three linear structures and their operations.
Exact nameWhat it doesHow to tell it apart
StackExposes the top: push, pop, peek.Last in, first out.
QueueInserts at the tail, removes at the head: enqueue, dequeue, peek.First in, first out.
Priority queueSame operation names as a queue, but dequeue returns the best priority.Order depends on priority, not arrival.

A list is not one of the three: it allows access at any position. It is used to implement them.

🧪 Worked examples
Trace these by hand before moving on.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5.1

Balanced braces with a stack

The problem

Decide whether { ( ) } is balanced.

The trace
SymbolActionStack (top at right)
{push{
(push{ (
)pop (, types match{
}pop {, types matchempty
The lesson

Balanced: every closing symbol matched the top, and the stack ended empty.

WORKED EXAMPLE 5.2

Queue from two stacks

The problem

Enqueue A, B, C, then dequeue.

The trace
  • IN is [A, B, C] with C on top; OUT is empty.
  • Dequeue finds OUT empty, so pop IN and push onto OUT: OUT becomes [C, B, A] with A on top.
  • Pop OUT: returns A, the oldest item.
The lesson

Reversing twice restores first-in, first-out order.

📝 In-class exercises
Attempt each one first, then open the answer.
1
Browser back, forward and visit. Stacks U = [C, B, A] (C on top), current page D, R empty. Run: back, back, forward, visit(E), back. Record U, current page and R after each action.
Show answer
Start: U [C, B, A], current D, R []. back: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. back: U [A], current B, R [C, D]. forward: U [B, A], current C, R [D]. visit(E): U [C, B, A], current E, R [] (visit clears R). back: U [B, A], current C, R [E]. Forward is available because R is not empty and holds E.
2
Round-robin help desk. Queue [(A, 5), (B, 2), (C, 4)], head first. Each turn dequeues the head, processes min(2, remaining) minutes, then finishes the job or enqueues it at the tail. Give the completion order and number of turns.
Show answer
Turn 1: A 5 to 3, queue [B2, C4, A3]. Turn 2: B finishes. Turn 3: C 4 to 2, queue [A3, C2]. Turn 4: A 3 to 1, queue [C2, A1]. Turn 5: C finishes. Turn 6: A finishes. Completion order B, C, A in 6 turns. In general the turns equal Σ ⌈tᵢ/2⌉ and the number of queue operations is O(Σ tᵢ) for a fixed quantum.
3
Remove adjacent duplicates. Process ABBACA left to right with a stack: pop if the character equals the top, otherwise push.
Show answer
Stack after each character: [A], [A, B], [A] (second B cancels), [] (A cancels), [C], [C, A]. Final string, bottom to top: CA. Removing one pair can expose a new equal pair underneath, which the stack handles automatically. Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n).
4
Priority help desk. Smaller number is higher priority; ties go to the earlier arrival. Start with A(3), B(1), C(2). Perform: enqueue D(1); dequeue; enqueue E(2); dequeue; dequeue.
Show answer
After enqueue D(1): next order B, D, C, A. Dequeue returns B. Enqueue E(2): order D, C, E, A. Dequeue returns D. Dequeue returns C. The remaining queue is E(2), A(3), so the complete removal sequence is B, D, C, E, A.
5
Queue from two stacks. enqueue pushes onto IN. dequeue pops OUT, but if OUT is empty it first moves every IN value onto OUT. Trace: enqueue A, B, C, dequeue, enqueue D, dequeue, dequeue, enqueue E, dequeue.
Show answer
Enqueues leave IN [A, B, C]. First dequeue transfers, so OUT [C, B] after returning A. Enqueue D gives IN [D]. Dequeue returns B, then C (OUT empties). Enqueue E gives IN [D, E]. The last dequeue transfers and returns D, leaving OUT [E], so the next item is E. One dequeue is O(n) in the worst case (a transfer), but each element moves at most once, so the amortised cost is O(1) per operation. Auxiliary space O(n).
📚 Tutorial questions
Tier-1 questions from the tutorial, with the answer key.
1
Push and pop letters. A letter means push and * means pop. For the sequence A R D G * O * C A R E L D O * * C F U L * * C L O C * K * * *, give the letters popped from an initially empty stack, and the letters dequeued if a letter means enqueue and * means dequeue.
Show answer
Stack: GOODLUCKOL. Queue: ARDGOCAREL.
2
Weird queue. What queue does do_weird_stuff(6) return? For i in range(n): if i is odd, dequeue x and enqueue x + i; otherwise enqueue i.
Show answer
[4, 4, 7], with 4 at the head. Trace: [0], [1], [1, 2], [2, 4], [2, 4, 4], [4, 4, 7].
3
Which pop sequences are possible?. Numbers 1 to n are pushed in increasing order, with pops at any time. Give operations that print 1 3 5 4 2. Is there a sequence that cannot occur?
Show answer
Push 1, pop (1); push 2, push 3, pop (3); push 4, push 5, pop (5), pop (4), pop (2). Impossible example: 1 5 4 2 3. Once a value n₃ is popped, two smaller values that were pushed earlier cannot come out in increasing order, so 3, 1, 2 can never occur.
4
Invert, and delete, using the other structure. Invert a queue using a stack; invert a stack using a queue; delete one element from a stack using a queue while keeping the rest in order.
Show answer
Invert the queue: dequeue everything onto the stack, then pop everything back into the queue. Invert the stack: pop everything into the queue, then dequeue everything back onto the stack. Delete from the stack: pop each element into the queue unless it is the one to delete; push everything back (now reversed); pop into the queue again; push back (original order restored without the deleted element).
5
Non-recursive factorial. Convert the recursive factorial into a version that uses a stack.
Show answer
Push n; result = 1; while the stack is not empty, pop m, result *= m, and if m > 1 push m − 1. Return result.
⚡ Quick examples
Choosing the end of the array
PointPut the stack top at the end of the list.
Exampleappend() and pop() without an index.
ExplanationNo other item has to shift.
Priority queue trade-off
PointUnsorted list: cheap insert, costly removal.
ExampleSorted list: costly insert, cheap removal.
ExplanationPick by whether you insert or remove more often.
✅ This chapter in 30 seconds
  • An ADT is defined by its operations, not its implementation.
  • Stack is last in, first out; queue is first in, first out.
  • Put the stack top at the end of the array for O(1) push and pop.
  • An array queue has O(n) dequeue from the front.
  • A priority queue returns the best priority; a min-heap gives O(log n) for both ends.
  • A queue can be built from two stacks with amortised O(1) dequeue.
🃏 Flip to recall
Say the answer out loud first, then tap the card.
LIFO or FIFO: stack?tap to flip
LIFO: last in, first out.
Cost of dequeue in a plain array queuetap to flip
O(n): the remaining items shift down.
Why does a two-stack queue reverse twice?tap to flip
Moving items from IN to OUT reverses the order, restoring FIFO.

O(log n) enqueue and dequeue, O(1) peek.
➡ Where next? Linear structures expose one end. Trees add branching, and keep sorted order usable.
