mcq.q: A standard deck has 4 suits. What is the minimum number of cards you must draw to guarantee at least 3 cards of the same suit?
mcq.e: Pigeonhole: k(m−1)+1 = 4×2+1 = 9. With 8 cards you could hold exactly 2 of each suit.

mcq.q: 100 people are in a room. What is the largest number *n* such that at least *n* of them are guaranteed to share a birth month?
mcq.e: 12 months × 8 = 96 < 100, so some month has at least 9 people. (97 people are already enough.)

mcq.q: A licence plate has 3 letters (A–Z) followed by 4 digits (0–9). Letters and digits may repeat. How many plates are possible?
mcq.e: Seven independent positions, so the product rule gives 26³ × 10⁴ = 175,760,000.

mcq.q: Same plate format as Q3, but no letter may repeat and no digit may repeat. How many plates are possible?
mcq.e: Order matters (plates), so use permutations: P(26,3) × P(10,4) = 15,600 × 5,040 = 78,624,000. B is the combination mistake C(26,3)×C(10,4).

mcq.q: A set meal is either a starter + main or a main + dessert. There are 5 starters, 8 mains and 4 desserts. How many different set meals?
mcq.e: Product rule inside each option: 5×8 = 40 and 8×4 = 32. The two options cannot overlap (one has a starter, the other a dessert), so the sum rule gives 72.

mcq.q: In a class of 40, 25 take Python, 18 take Java and 8 take both. How many take neither?
mcq.e: Inclusion–exclusion: |P ∪ J| = 25 + 18 − 8 = 35. Neither = 40 − 35 = 5.

mcq.q: A PIN has 4 digits (0–9, leading zeros allowed). How many PINs contain at least one repeated digit?
mcq.e: Complement rule: total 10⁴ = 10,000 minus all-distinct 10×9×8×7 = 5,040 → 4,960.

mcq.q: How many 3-letter strings (letters A–Z, repeats allowed) contain at least one vowel (A, E, I, O, U)?
mcq.e: Complement: 26³ − 21³ = 17,576 − 9,261 = 8,315 (21 consonants).

mcq.q: Ten runners finish a race. In how many ways can the gold, silver and bronze medals be awarded?
mcq.e: Swap test: gold and silver are different outcomes → permutation. P(10,3) = 10×9×8 = 720.

mcq.q: A committee of 4 (no special roles) is chosen from 12 people. How many committees?
mcq.e: Order does not matter: C(12,4) = 495. C is P(12,4), which overcounts by 4! = 24.

mcq.q: A group has 5 men and 6 women. How many committees of 4 contain exactly 2 women?
mcq.e: C(6,2) × C(5,2) = 15 × 10 = 150 (product rule on two independent choices).

mcq.q: Same group (5 men, 6 women). How many committees of 4 contain at least one woman?
mcq.e: Complement: all committees C(11,4) = 330 minus all-men committees C(5,4) = 5 → 325.

mcq.q: 7 different books are placed on a shelf. Three of them (a trilogy) must be next to each other, in any order. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Block method: block + 4 others = 5 objects → 5! = 120, times 3! = 6 internal orders = 720. (1,440 would be 6!×2.)

mcq.q: Same 7 books, but the trilogy must be together in the order Vol 1, Vol 2, Vol 3. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: The block has only one internal order, so just 5! = 120.

mcq.q: 5 boys and 3 girls stand in a row (all different people). No two girls may stand next to each other. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Gap method: arrange the boys 5! = 120, creating 6 gaps. Choose 3 gaps C(6,3) = 20 and arrange the girls 3! = 6. 120×20×6 = 14,400. (C = forgetting to arrange the girls.)

mcq.q: 7 different people sit around a round table. Rotations count as the same arrangement. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Fix one person, arrange the other 6: (7−1)! = 720.

mcq.q: 7 different people sit around a round table (rotations are the same). Two particular people, Amy and Ben, must sit next to each other. How many arrangements?
mcq.e: Treat Amy+Ben as one block → 6 objects in a circle → (6−1)! = 120, times 2! for the block's internal order = 240. (B forgets the circular reduction.)

mcq.q: A bracelet is made from 6 different beads. Two bracelets are the same if one can be rotated or flipped over to match the other. How many different bracelets?
mcq.e: Circular arrangements (6−1)! = 120; reflections are identified in pairs, so divide by 2: 60.

mcq.q: How many 4-digit numbers (1000 to 9999) are there if digits may repeat?
mcq.e: First digit 9 choices (not 0), each of the other three 10 choices: 9×10³. C (9×9×8×7) is the all-distinct count.

mcq.q: How many 3-digit numbers (100 to 999) have all different digits and are even?
mcq.e:
Split by the last digit:
• Last digit 0: first digit 9 choices, middle 8 → 72.
• Last digit 2, 4, 6 or 8 (4 choices): first digit can't be 0 or the last digit → 8 choices; middle digit can't be either used digit → 8 choices → 4×8×8 = 256.
Total 72 + 256 = 328 (sum rule over disjoint cases). C (648) is all 3-digit numbers with distinct digits, ignoring "even".

mcq.q: 12 people at a party each shake hands exactly once with every other person. How many handshakes?
mcq.e: A handshake is an unordered pair: C(12,2) = 66.

mcq.q: How many 8-bit binary strings start with 1 or end with 00?
mcq.e: Inclusion–exclusion: start with 1 = 2⁷ = 128; end with 00 = 2⁶ = 64; both = 2⁵ = 32. 128 + 64 − 32 = 160.

mcq.q: How many 8-bit binary strings contain exactly three 1s?
mcq.e: Choose which 3 of the 8 positions hold a 1: C(8,3) = 56. (C is P(8,3).)

mcq.q:
What is the time complexity of this merge-sort-style function, where combining the two sorted halves takes O(n)?
def m(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left = m(a[:mid])
    right = m(a[mid:])
    return combine(left, right)   # O(n)
mcq.e: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): log n levels, each doing O(n) total work → n log n.

mcq.e: Postorder = left, right, parent: left subtree 1, 4, 7, 6, 3; right subtree 13, 14, 10; then 8.

mcq.q: The tree is a binary search tree. Which traversal visits the keys in ascending order?
mcq.e: Inorder (left, parent, right) on a BST gives 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14.

mcq.q: How many key comparisons are needed to search for 7 in the BST?
mcq.e: The path is 8 → 3 → 6 → 7, so 4 nodes are compared.

mcq.q: The root (8) is removed. It has two children. Which pair lists the values that could replace it while keeping the BST ordering valid?
mcq.e: The replacement is either the right-most node of the left subtree (3 → 6 → 7, so 7) or the left-most node of the right subtree (10 has no left child, so 10).

mcq.e: Sorted insertion makes every node the right child of the previous one (a linked list), so searching for 50 compares all 5 nodes. Inserting 30 first, then the middles of each half, would give a balanced tree instead.

mcq.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree with 5 levels (root is level 1)?
mcq.e: Each level can double: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 2⁵ − 1 = 31.

mcq.e: Height ≈ ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10, and the worst-case comparisons equal the tree's height.

mcq.e: Swaps = number of inversions: 5 is before 2, 4, 1, 3 (4); 2 before 1 (1); 4 before 1, 3 (2); 6 before 1, 3 (2). Total 9.

mcq.q: How many comparisons does insertion sort make on an already sorted list of 10 elements?
mcq.e: Each of the 9 later elements is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put (best case O(n)).

mcq.q: How many comparisons does selection sort make to sort 8 elements (any input order)?
mcq.e: 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = n(n−1)/2 = 28, regardless of the order of the input.

mcq.q: Selection sort is applied to [64, 25, 12, 22, 11]. What does the array look like after two passes?
mcq.e: Pass 1: smallest is 11, swap with 64 → [11, 25, 12, 22, 64]. Pass 2: smallest of the rest is 12, swap with 25 → [11, 12, 25, 22, 64]. (B is after one pass.)

mcq.e: Comparisons: 2v1, 2v6, 5v6, 9v6, 9v7, 9v10. After 9 is taken the first list is empty, so 10 is copied without a comparison.

mcq.e: M1 has 4 choices, M2 has 3, M3 has 2 and M4 has 1, so 4·3·2·1 = ⁴P₄ = 24. Choosing the order of the women already fixes who pairs with whom, so multiplying by another ⁴P₄ double-counts.

mcq.q: Mock exam Q9. Which statement is false?
o: Binary search requires a sorted array.
The best case of binary search is O(1).
Given the same inputs, an O(n²) algorithm is always faster than an O(2ⁿ) algorithm.
A priority queue returns the highest-priority element on dequeue and peek.

mcq.e: Big-O describes growth for large n, not exact running time. For small n, or with large constants, an O(2ⁿ) algorithm can be quicker, so "always" makes the statement false. The other statements are true.

mcq.q: Mock exam Q15. What is the best-case time complexity of selection sort?
mcq.e: Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part, so it makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons in every case. Insertion sort is the one with an O(n) best case.

mcq.q: Mock exam Q16. What is the worst-case time complexity of selection sort?
mcq.e: The comparison count is n(n−1)/2 for every input, so the worst case is also O(n²).

mcq.q: Mock exam Q17. How many swaps does selection sort make in its best case, an already sorted list?
mcq.e: It swaps only when the current position does not already hold the smallest remaining item. A sorted list needs no swaps, although it still makes n(n−1)/2 comparisons. The worst case is at most n − 1 swaps.

wr.q: Mock exam Q6. Write the recursive equivalent of the iterative `isSorted(a)`.
wr.a:
Index version, O(n):

def isSorted(a, i=0):
    if i >= len(a) - 1:       # 0 or 1 elements left: sorted
        return True
    if a[i] > a[i+1]:         # out-of-order pair
        return False
    return isSorted(a, i + 1) # check the rest

The slicing version return a[0] < a[1] and isSorted(a[1:]) is also acceptable but copies lists, so it costs O(n²).

Marking points: correct base case, comparison of adjacent elements, returning False on a violation, and a recursive call on a smaller problem.

wr.q: Mock exam Q8. Sorting with two stacks. Inside the loop while currentInt < topStack, the top of stack is moved to tempstack. Fill in the two blanks: (1) how to look at the new top of stack without removing it, and (2) how to move the larger elements back.

Answer 1: stack[-1], a peek. stack.pop() would delete the element.

Answer 2: stack.append(tempstack.pop()). The larger elements went to tempstack largest-first, so the smallest of them is on top and must sit just above currentInt. Popping them one by one restores ascending order.

Trace on [3,1,2] gives [1,2,3]. Worst case is O(n²).

wr.q:
Mock exam Q19. Complete the recursive merge. The blanks are answer 1, answer 2 and answer 3.
def merge3(a1, a2, i=0, j=0):
    if i < len(a1) or j < len(a2):
        if (j == len(a2)) or (i < len(a1) and a1[i] < a2[j]):
            return [ a1[i] ] + merge3(__answer1__)
        else:
            return [ a2[j] ] + merge3(__answer2__)
    return __answer3__
wr.a:
Answer 1: a1, a2, i+1, j
Answer 2: a1, a2, i, j+1
Answer 3: []

i and j replace the loop variables of the iterative merge. Taking a1[i] advances i, and taking a2[j] advances j. When both lists are exhausted the base case returns the empty list, the identity for +. Common mistakes: forgetting to pass a1, a2, returning None, and writing i++.

wr.q:
Mock exam Q20. Complete the stack-based merge. The stack holds the state (i, j) that the recursive version passes as arguments.
def stk_merge3(a1, a2):
    stk = Stack(); stk.push(0); stk.push(0)
    r = []
    while stk.count() > 0:
        i = stk.pop(); j = stk.pop()
        if i < len(a1) or j < len(a2):
            if (j == len(a2)) or (i < len(a1) and a1[i] < a2[j]):
                r.append(a1[i]); stk.push(j); stk.push(i+1)
            else:
                r.append(__answer1__)
                stk.push(__answer2__)
                stk.push(__answer3__)
    return r
wr.a:
Answer 1: a2[j]
Answer 2: j+1
Answer 3: i

Push order matters: i is popped first and then j, so j is pushed first and i last. In the else branch j advances and i is unchanged. When neither index is in range nothing is pushed, the stack empties and the loop ends.

wr.q: Mock exam Q22. Describe a better algorithm than brute force for the closest pair of integers in a list of `n` integers, with its worst-case complexity.
wr.a:
Sort, then compare adjacent elements: O(n log n).

def closest_pair(a):
    b = sorted(a)                  # merge sort: O(n log n)
    best_pair, best_dist = (b[0], b[1]), b[1] - b[0]
    for k in range(1, len(b) - 1): # one pass: O(n)
        d = b[k+1] - b[k]
        if d < best_dist:
            best_dist, best_pair = d, (b[k], b[k+1])
    return best_pair

After sorting, the closest pair must be adjacent: if x < y < z then |x−z| is at least as large as both |x−y| and |y−z|. The total is O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan. With insertion or selection sort the total would be O(n²), no better than brute force.
